title: The Marginal Job Trap: Why the Next Sale Isn't Always as Profitable as the Last One
linkedin:
Revenue is climbing again after EOFY. For a lot of owners, that feels like proof the year has turned a corner.

But here's what the P&L doesn't say out loud: the next job you take on isn't automatically as profitable as the last one.

We see this constantly with owner-led businesses once they're running close to capacity. A trade business fits in one more job than the crew can comfortably handle, and it gets finished through paid overtime or a subcontractor charging a premium for short notice. A professional services firm accepts one more client than the team can service properly, and a partner ends up doing the work personally, unbilled, at their most valuable hour.

None of this shows up as a line item called "cost of growth." It's scattered through the P&L as overtime, subcontractor fees, freight and rework, easy to miss until someone adds it up job by job.

The fix isn't always a pricing conversation, even though that's where owners usually look first. It's a capacity conversation. The number worth tracking isn't your average gross margin, it's the contribution margin on the specific job in front of you, priced honestly for what it actually costs to fit in.

Growth shouldn't slow down. It just needs a clear-eyed view of which growth is adding to profit and which is quietly diluting it.

If your calendar has been filling up since EOFY, you're not alone. Enquiries tend to lift for East Coast SMEs through August as the new financial year gets underway, and a busier diary usually feels like good news.

One thing worth checking before you say yes to the next job or client: is it actually as profitable as the work you're already doing? Once a team is running close to capacity, extra work often gets delivered through overtime, a subcontractor charging more for short notice, or the owner stepping back into delivery themselves to cover the gap. None of that shows up as its own cost on the P&L. It just quietly eats into the margin, job by job.

The businesses that handle this well aren't slowing down growth. They're checking the profitability of the next piece of work before it lands on the calendar, not after, using the actual cost of delivering it rather than the average across the year.

If growth has picked up for your business this month, it's worth a proper look at whether that growth is adding to profit or just adding to revenue. Read the full piece on the ProfitPulse blog for a practical way to check.
